title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
summary: Command and Scripting Interpreter describes the abuse of native command interpreters and scripting runtimes to execute code on a target host, chain further actions, and stage additional payloads without necessarily writing a conventional executable to disk. The parent technique covers interpreters such as PowerShell, the Windows command shell, Unix shells, Python, JavaScript engines and platform-specific automation hosts, and it appears on Windows, Linux, macOS, network appliances and inside container and cloud execution contexts wherever a shell or runtime is reachable. At a mechanism level the adversary runs an interpreter interactively, passes commands as arguments, or loads script content from a local file, a remote share, or an encoded blob that is decoded into memory at execution time. The telemetry this produces is rich but noisy: process creation records showing interpreter binaries with unusual parent processes, command lines containing encoded or obfuscated arguments, script block and module logging on Windows, process accounting and execve audit records on Linux, shell history files, and the child processes the interpreter subsequently spawns. Investigators separate malicious from benign use by examining the parent-child relationship, the user and session context, the working directory and destination of any download, whether the interpreter was launched by a service or scheduled task, whether logging captured the full script content, and whether the same interpreter and argument pattern recurs across hosts at a rate that matches an automated campaign rather than an administrator. Change windows, software deployment tooling and signed management agents explain a large share of legitimate interpreter invocations, so the bar for escalation should be unusual lineage, unusual content or unusual timing rather than the mere presence of the interpreter.
objectives: Describe how interpreters such as PowerShell, the Windows command shell and Unix shells are invoked and how their command lines differ from routine administrative use.
Identify the process-creation, script-block, module and shell-history telemetry that records interpreter execution across Windows and Linux estates.
Explain how encoded or obfuscated interpreter arguments are surfaced in logging and where visibility gaps typically appear.
Distinguish adversary interpreter abuse from legitimate automation, configuration management and software deployment activity.
Design detection logic that keys on process lineage, argument content and cross-host recurrence rather than on interpreter presence alone.
Assess how interpreter logging configuration and constrained language modes change both visibility and attacker cost.
